Imagine not just a like button but a eye button that would list all the people that looked. 

Creepy or the next substack surveillance  move? 

So I asked my Chat GTP ….

😂 

Honestly? Both. 😂

As a feature, an 👁️ “who viewed this” button would be wildly compelling. It would turn passive readership into visible social behavior.

But the second you can see exactly who looked, the psychological contract changes.

Right now:

Like = “I publicly acknowledge this.”View = “I privately consumed this.”

An eye button would basically say:



“You thought you were lurking anonymously? Absolutely not.”

And THAT is where the creepiness begins.

I could also see the very Substack-y version being:

👁 47 people viewed this    

-                                                                  

Want to know who? 

Upgrade to Substack Pro™.

😂

But there's an interesting middle ground: show the number of views, but not the identities. That gives writers useful feedback without turning every post into a tiny surveillance dashboard.

Or, if they really wanted to embrace chaos:

👁 Who's Watching





12 subscribers



4 non-subscribers



3 people who absolutely refuse to like anything



1 person who has read this 7 times



1 person you blocked in 2024 👀

Now THAT would be the next Substack surveillance move.

The Midnight Pavilion

Everyone in the village believed the pavilion had been built for dances.

By day, it sat quietly in the center of the Moonflower Garden, wrapped in climbing roses and silver vines. White lilies surrounded its marble columns, and crystal lanterns hung from the ceiling like frozen stars.

Visitors came to admire the flowers.

Poets came to write.

Lovers came to make promises.

No one noticed the clock.

It was hidden beneath the pavilion floor, buried deep below the roots of the moonflowers.

A clock older than history.

A clock that did not count hours.

It counted destinations.

Every night at exactly midnight, the pavilion awakened.

The lanterns filled with violet light.

The roses closed.

The moonflowers opened.

And the marble floor began to hum.

Those standing beneath the pavilion at the stroke of midnight would vanish.

Not disappear.

Travel.

The strange thing was that the pavilion never asked where you wanted to go.

It decided for you.

And for reasons no one understood, its first destination was almost always Ancient Egypt.

Travelers would step beneath the pavilion surrounded by roses and emerge moments later beneath a blazing desert sun.

Golden sand stretched endlessly toward the horizon.

Great temples shimmered in the distance.

The Nile sparkled like liquid emerald beneath the stars.

Some found themselves walking through bustling markets filled with perfumes and lapis jewelry.

Others stood among colossal statues whose eyes seemed older than time itself.

A few lucky travelers witnessed the pyramids while they were still new.

No one knew why the pavilion favored Egypt.

Some believed an ancient priestess had built it.

Others claimed the pavilion itself had first been created there thousands of years ago and simply liked returning home.

The most curious theory belonged to Alice.

Alice had discovered the pavilion accidentally.

One moonlit evening she wandered across a small bridge that crossed a silver stream winding through the midnight garden.

Moonflowers glowed along the water's edge.

Fireflies floated between the roses.

The air smelled faintly of jasmine and secrets.

At the center of the garden stood the pavilion.

Its crystal lanterns were already glowing.

Alice checked her pocket watch.

11:59.

"That seems suspicious," she whispered.

The clock struck midnight.

The lanterns burst into brilliant starlight.

The marble floor beneath her feet transformed into a swirling galaxy.

Then the entire pavilion vanished.

A moment later Alice found herself standing beneath a sky unlike any she had ever seen.

The Milky Way stretched across the heavens.

Massive pyramids towered before her.

Golden torches flickered along stone pathways.

And somewhere beyond the dunes, music echoed through the desert night.

Ancient Egypt.

Again.

The pavilion seemed very proud of itself.

"Oh," Alice sighed.

"Not Egypt again."

The wind answered by scattering glowing desert flowers across the sand.

Alice laughed.

Apparently even magical time-travel pavilions had favorite destinations.

Still, she stayed.

Because everyone knew the secret.

If you survived Egypt until the next midnight...

The pavilion would open again.

And then it could take you absolutely anywhere.

Victorian London.

Atlantis.

A crystal city on the moon.

A forgotten library hidden between centuries.

The last garden at the end of time.

Or a place no map had ever named.

The pavilion never explained its choices.

It simply waited beneath the moonflowers.

Patient.

Silent.

Counting destinations.

And every midnight, somewhere in the garden, another curious traveler stepped beneath its glowing roof and wondered where they might wake up next.

The candles dim.

The stars fade.

The fireplace settles into glowing coals.

And the girl vanishes.

BEAUTY BEGINS AT THE BERRY

The incredible story of the coffee cherry. ♡

Before it becomes the aromatic brew we love, coffee starts as a vibrant little fruit called a coffee cherry.

Grown on coffee trees in tropical regions, these cherries hold two seeds (coffee beans) inside.

It takes care, patience, and the perfect climate to bring them to life.

♡

THE JOURNEY OF THE CHERRY

1. GROWN WITH CARE

Coffee trees take 3–4 years to produce cherries.

2. HAND-PICKED

Ripe cherries are carefully picked, usually by hand.

3. PROCESSED

The cherries are washed, fermented, and dried to reveal the beans.

4. ROASTED TO PERFECTION

Heat unlocks the flavor, aroma, and magic.

5. BREWED WITH LOVE

And finally, it's ready for your cup.

“When Ice Cream Belonged to Kings”

Before freezers hummed in suburban kitchens and neon parlors glowed at midnight, frozen cream was a forbidden luxury.

In ancient Persia, royal courts chilled sweetened rosewater in underground ice houses. Roman emperors sent servants racing to mountaintops for snow. In candlelit European castles, frozen desserts appeared only during lavish feasts — shimmering in silver bowls beside jewels, velvet, and wine.

Ice cream was not comfort food.

It was spectacle.

A symbol of wealth so extravagant that entire kingdoms engineered underground chambers simply to preserve ice through summer heat.

Some historians believe King Charles I of England tried to keep his frozen cream recipe secret from the public — preserving it as a privilege of royalty alone.

And perhaps that mystery still lingers.

Even now, ice cream feels strangely ceremonial: the silver spoon, the midnight craving, the melting moment before disappearance.

A temporary sweetness. A beautiful collapse.
